query: Which material can be used for enhanced catalytic activity and durability toward HER and HOR, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A compositionally engineered, Pt‐based high-entropy alloy catalyst, in which Pt is alloyed with several secondary elements, will exhibit both enhanced intrinsic HER/HOR activity and superior long-term durability compared to conventional Pt catalysts.
generation.material_initial_state: Traditional Pt-based catalysts that offer high catalytic activity but suffer from durability issues such as degradation and Pt dissolution under electrochemical conditions.
generation.intervention: Synthesize a high-entropy alloy catalyst that incorporates Pt along with several selected secondary elements (for example, Ni, Co, Ru, and Mo) in near-equiatomic or compositionally optimized ratios.
generation.conditions: Electrochemical environments typical of fuel cells and electrolyzers (acidic or alkaline media, ambient to moderate operating temperatures) where HER and HOR are performed.
generation.structural_mediator: A stabilized solid-solution structure with tailored surface electronic properties and resistance to corrosive oxidation/dissolution due to the multi-element (high-entropy) composition.
generation.mechanism: Alloying Pt with additional elements alters the electronic structure (thereby modifying adsorption energies of hydrogen intermediates) and increases phase stability, which together reduce degradation mechanisms and improve catalytic kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: The engineered Pt-based high-entropy alloy catalyst will show an improved HER/HOR performance (with activity gains on the order of approximately 10–20% relative to conventional Pt) and a notably slower degradation rate under extended electrochemical cycling.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (activity and durability) of standard Pt catalysts under similar electrochemical operating conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are contingent upon achieving an optimal composition; excessive dilution of Pt active sites or unfavorable phase segregations could negate improvements, and performance may vary with electrolyte pH and temperature.
generation.uncertainty: The precise elemental ratios and processing conditions needed to achieve the desired balance between catalytic activity and durability remain to be determined, and scalability of the synthesis may affect reproducibility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare the proposed Pt-based high-entropy alloy catalyst and a control standard Pt catalyst. Perform electrochemical testing under identical conditions (using polarization curves, cyclic voltammetry, and accelerated degradation tests) to record HER/HOR activities and durability over prolonged cycling. Compare the long-term performance (activity retention and structural integrity) of both catalysts.
measurements: Polarization curves to assess HER/HOR kinetics
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to analyze charge transfer
Accelerated degradation testing (ADT) to evaluate durability
Surface analysis (e.g., XPS, TEM) pre- and post-cycling to detect structural and compositional changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Pt-based high-entropy alloy catalyst does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in both catalytic activity (e.g., at least 10–20% increase in current density at relevant overpotentials) and durability (e.g., slower degradation rates over ADT) compared to the conventional Pt catalyst, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. decision.trend: Historically, electrocatalyst design has been dominated by Pt-based materials that offer excellent hydrogen reaction kinetics but are hampered by durability issues under operating conditions. Early attempts then moved to Pt‐alloys to improve longevity; however, these modifications only partially resolved the degradation challenges. In parallel, across alloy research (e.g., in high‐entropy and refractory systems), researchers have shown that careful compositional tuning can induce phase stability and resilience even under harsh environments. Although these alloy studies were chiefly directed at mechanical or high-temperature applications, they illustrate the power of a composition-change approach to simultaneously modulate activity (via the electronic structure) and durability (via phase stability and resistance to degradation).
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved challenge in HER/HOR catalysis remains the coexistence of high intrinsic catalytic activity with long-term resistance to degradation. Existing Pt-based systems still present a trade-off where enhanced activity comes at the cost of durability under aggressive electrochemical conditions.
decision.why: Following the trend that shows alloying as an effective method to improve durability in demanding environments, the most plausible next step is to develop a compositionally engineered catalyst. Specifically, an experimental study that designs and tests a novel alloy—potentially a high-entropy or intermetallic variant incorporating Pt with carefully chosen secondary elements—can tailor the electronic structure to boost HER/HOR kinetics while forming a stable surface phase resistant to degradation. This approach directly addresses the open question by leveraging the material composition lever, a niche move already validated by analogous studies in other fields.
